narrative.text: The acknowledgements for the key populations guidelines, naming the GRADE methodologist, the Guideline Development Group co-chairs and members, external reviewers and other contributors. It notes funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and PEPFAR.
A list of acronyms and abbreviations used in the key populations guidelines, covering terms such as ART, HBV, HCV, PrEP, OAMT, NSP and agency names.

A glossary defining terms used in the key populations guidelines, from acute hepatitis C and adolescents through to unprotected sex. It explains age-related terms such as adolescents, youth and young people and notes that adolescents may also belong to key population groups. Other entries define the key populations and prevention concepts, for example that effective ART with viral suppression prevents sexual transmission of HIV.

The executive summary, stating that the guidelines set out a public health response to HIV, viral hepatitis and STIs for five key populations and combine new and existing WHO recommendations. It explains why the same five groups are used across the three disease areas, citing shared structural barriers, risk behaviours and interventions. It then outlines how interventions are classed as essential for impact, essential for broader health, or supportive.

A summary list of recommended interventions, grouped into enabling interventions such as removing punitive laws and addressing violence, health interventions for prevention, diagnosis and treatment, and broader health interventions such as mental health, contraception and gender-affirming care.
A chapter 1 divider page with only the guideline title and navigation labels.

Explains that earlier WHO key population guidelines covered only HIV, but the five key populations are also disproportionately affected by viral hepatitis and STIs, creating syndemics. It states that these guidelines focus on the same five groups across all three disease areas and introduces the reasons for doing so.

Completes the reasons for focusing on the five key populations and notes that people may belong to several groups or move in and out of them over time. It stresses that poor coverage and quality of services undermine national responses and that countries should prioritize these populations, with a figure showing biological, behavioural and social factors driving transmission.

Sets out the epidemiological case for focusing HIV, hepatitis and STI programmes on key populations, citing models showing that preventing infections in these groups has outsized impact on population transmission. It describes how the infections interact as syndemics, for example STIs increasing HIV infectiousness and acquisition and women with HIV facing higher cervical cancer risk.

Links the response in key populations to SDG target 3.3 and UNAIDS 2025 coverage targets, and presents a theory of change for reaching the 2030 goals. It covers ensuring access at scale, reducing structural barriers, funding effective packages, community empowerment and service delivery approaches such as decentralization and integration.
States the scope of the guidelines: a public health response for five key populations, combining new and existing recommendations and setting out prioritized intervention packages.

Lists the four objectives of the updated key population guidelines, from developing new evidence-based recommendations to outlining priority service packages, given the high burden of infections and persistent barriers these populations face.

Identifies the intended audience as national HIV, hepatitis and STI programme managers, prison health authorities and other policy-makers, and endorses the Global AIDS Strategy targets for community-led service delivery. It adds managers of related services, civil society, law enforcement, advocates and funders as secondary audiences.

Sets out the principles behind WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis and STIs for key populations, starting with human rights such as non-discrimination and access to quality health services and medicines. It also states the guidelines' commitment to the meaningful involvement of people living with HIV and of key populations in the response.

Explains how to use the consolidated guideline, noting that most recommendations come from other WHO documents that are cited rather than repeated, that new or updated 2021/2022 recommendations are marked with a star, and that supporting evidence is in Web Annexes A–D.
A chapter divider page carrying the guideline's running title and its chapter navigation headings.

Gives an overview of how the key populations guidelines were developed by WHO's Global HIV, Hepatitis and STIs Programmes using the WHO guideline handbook and GRADE, as an update of the 2014/2016 guidelines that now also covers viral hepatitis and STIs.

Describes the groups that guided development of the key populations guidelines, starting with a WHO steering group led by the Testing, Prevention and Population Unit with staff from several departments. It outlines the roles of the other groups and notes that funders and partner organizations attended the guideline meeting as observers.

Describes how competing interests of external contributors were managed, including declaration of interest forms, reviews of CVs and online searches, and a public comment period on the proposed membership. One member's interest led to their partial exclusion from decisions on hepatitis C treatment.

Explains how the scope of the update to the 2016 key populations guidelines was set, aiming to add viral hepatitis and STI recommendations, propose prioritized intervention packages per key population and stress critical enablers. It describes the review of existing recommendations and consultations, after which participants endorsed the proposed structure.

Describes a WHO-commissioned qualitative study of key populations' values and preferences, carried out by four global key population networks through 61 interviews and 32 focus groups. It notes that people in prisons could not be included and that the findings were combined into a single report in Web Annex B.

Explains how interventions were sorted into prioritized packages for each key population: essential enabling interventions, essential health interventions, broader interventions important for universal coverage, and supportive interventions such as demand creation and education.
States that the guidelines will be updated as evidence and country experience require, and describes dissemination online, in print on demand and through journal articles, policy briefs and apps.
A chapter divider page showing only the guideline's running title and page number.

Introduces the chapter on critical enablers, stating that HIV, hepatitis and STI epidemics among key populations are driven by criminalizing laws, stigma, discrimination, violence and other rights violations that restrict access to services. It also notes particular barriers facing adolescents from key populations, including consent requirements.

Summarizes what key population networks reported about structural barriers, with criminalization, stigma and discrimination named as persistent obstacles to care and drivers of poor health, and trans people also citing barriers to legal gender recognition. It closes with targets for the share of services and programmes to be delivered by community-led organizations.

Introduces a chapter describing structural barriers to health services for key populations and the critical enablers to overcome them, with good-practice recommendations carried over from the 2014/2016 guidelines.

Discusses legal and policy barriers faced by key populations, stressing their entitlement to human rights and states' duty to uphold them without discrimination. It cites research showing that criminalization and policing harm health outcomes, such as higher HIV prevalence among sex workers where sex work is criminalized. It calls for ways to report rights violations beyond the police, such as paralegals, and for laws and policies to be reviewed with key populations' involvement.

Defines stigma and discrimination and describes how key populations face them because of behaviour, sexual orientation, gender identity or sex work, often compounded by living with HIV. It describes how this deters people from seeking care, and ends with a statement that health services should be available, accessible and acceptable to key populations on the basis of non-discrimination and the right to health.

Describes how legal, social and programme environments limit key populations' control over their health, and how young people in particular receive poor or conflicting information. It argues for community empowerment and for involving key populations as partners in designing and running services. It ends with a good practice statement calling for a package of interventions to strengthen community empowerment.

Describes the forms of violence experienced by key populations and who commits it, from partners and clients to police and service providers, and how gender norms, discrimination and harsh laws drive it. It sets out responses including prevention, support and redress. It ends with statements that violence should be prevented with key population-led organizations, monitored and reported.
A heading fragment for the section on the recommended package of interventions.
A chapter divider page showing only the guideline's running title and page number.

Introduces the chapter on recommended interventions, explaining that most recommendations come from existing WHO guidelines that are cited rather than repeated, while new ones are detailed in the methods annexes and packages by key population appear in Chapter 5.

Explains that the recommended interventions are not ranked and defines the categories used to label them, such as new and existing GRADE recommendations, good practice statements, SAGE positions and adapted wording.

Lists the enabling interventions considered essential for impact, starting with good practice statements on reviewing punitive laws and working towards decriminalizing drug use, sex work, same-sex activity and non-conforming gender identities. It continues with statements on reducing stigma and discrimination, community empowerment and addressing violence. Each statement is labelled by type and source.

Lists the essential health interventions for key populations, beginning with harm reduction recommendations on needle and syringe programmes, low dead-space syringes, opioid agonist maintenance treatment and naloxone. Further sections cover HIV prevention such as condoms, oral PrEP, long-acting injectable cabotegravir and post-exposure prophylaxis, along with prevention of hepatitis and STIs. Later parts address testing and treatment, including urgent ART for pregnant and breastfeeding people and syphilis treatment in pregnancy. Each recommendation is labelled by type, strength and certainty of evidence, with references to the source WHO guidelines.

Describes supportive interventions such as information, education and demand creation, noting no evidence was found that behavioural counselling to change risk behaviour is effective. It also introduces a new good practice statement linked to rights, with details given in Chapter 9.
A chapter divider page showing only the guideline's running title and page number.
Opens Chapter 5, which presents the recommended interventions as packages for each key population.

Sets out the recommended package for sex workers, defining them as adults who exchange sex for money or goods and describing how sex work varies. It reports sex workers' opposition to periodic presumptive treatment of STIs on health and ethical grounds, and explains why viral hepatitis services are included in their essential package. It also lists other priority needs such as sexual and reproductive health, cancer screening, mental health and substance use care.

Sets out the recommended package for people who inject drugs, defining the group and noting that much of the guidance also applies to other routes of drug use. It explains WHO's view of harm reduction, including needle and syringe programmes, opioid agonist maintenance treatment and naloxone. It also explains why STI services and TB prevention, screening and treatment are part of the package for this group.

Sets out the recommended package for men who have sex with men, defining the group and noting their higher burden of HIV, hepatitis and STIs, including hepatitis A outbreaks that vaccination could prevent. It stresses that structural barriers such as criminalization, stigma and violence must be addressed first, and lists the essential enabling and health interventions in the package.

Describes trans and gender diverse people as a key population in WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis and STIs, explaining the umbrella term and why they need distinct status in the HIV response. It notes high rates of violence, stigma in health care and related mental health problems such as depression, which reduce use of health services. It ends with the package of recommended interventions for this group, including sexual and reproductive health, mental health and substance use services.

Defines prisons and other closed settings and the people detained there, noting that most considerations may also apply to other detained groups and that prison staff can lack health services. It explains that people in prison carry a disproportionate burden of HIV, hepatitis B and C and TB, partly because of the criminalization of drug use and sex work. It ends with the package of recommended interventions for prisons, including TB prevention, screening and treatment.
A navigation header page introducing chapter 6 of the key populations guidelines.

Opens the service delivery chapter by setting out that health services for key populations should be available, accessible, acceptable and of good quality. It notes how COVID-19 disrupted HIV, hepatitis and STI services through diverted funds and access barriers. It lists the delivery strategies covered, such as integration, decentralization, online services, self-care and peer involvement.

Describes the central role of key populations in leading programmes and services, from outreach to helping peers stay in treatment. It cites qualitative research by four key population networks that strongly endorsed community-led services as a counter to stigma. It gives UNAIDS definitions of community-led organizations and responses and points to related WHO guidance.

Defines health service integration as delivering a continuum of prevention, testing and treatment across the health system, which suits people with complex needs. A table classifies types of integration, from organizational to service level, and links them to these guidelines.

Explains decentralization of health services to lower-level and community sites, which can reduce stigma, travel costs and waiting times for key populations. It cautions that some people may prefer hospitals for anonymity and points to related WHO guidance.

Defines differentiated service delivery as a client-centred approach that adapts where, when and by whom services are provided, with examples such as less frequent methadone collection and WHO recommendations on ART delivery.

Describes virtual interventions for key populations, such as online outreach, case management, self-test information and linkage to treatment, provided data privacy concerns are addressed. It outlines common categories of online interventions and their potential to reduce loss to follow-up. It ends by noting gaps in evidence from sex workers and people who inject drugs and referring to chapter 9 for details of the new recommendation.

Gives WHO's working definition of self-care and notes that it can empower key populations facing structural barriers. It lists recommended self-managed approaches such as emergency contraception, self-sampling for STIs and HIV and HCV self-testing.
A heading fragment for programme and service considerations for young key population groups.

Introduces the chapter on young key populations, which updates four 2015 WHO technical briefs and notes that considerations also apply to young people in detention, with a quote from a youth advocate.

Explains that young people aged 10 to 24 face structural and personal vulnerabilities that limit access to prevention, harm reduction and reproductive health services. It notes limited data but a higher burden of HIV and STIs among young key populations and rising HCV among young people who inject drugs and young men who have sex with men. It urges countries to review age of consent policies that block access to services.
Describes how the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child obliges states to protect under-18s and states that excluding them from HIV, STI and hepatitis services breaches their rights.

Sets out elements of successful programming for young key populations, including services that are friendly, confidential, integrated and supported by trained providers and peers. It stresses meaningful youth engagement based on shared power and respect for young people's differing needs and rights. It ends with calls for legal information and services and family counselling where parental consent is required.
A heading fragment for the chapter on decision-making, planning and monitoring of the response.
A navigation header page for chapter 8 of the key populations guidelines.
Introduces the chapter on developing the response, describing planning, decision-making and monitoring as an ongoing cycle adapted to the local context.

Explains that a situational analysis, involving local key population members, should guide the response even where data are limited. It lists what must be understood, from local epidemic dynamics to environments, needs and health systems. It also stresses diversity of risk within key populations and lists assessment tools such as a UNODC prison toolkit.

Notes that recommended intervention packages are effective across settings but that local factors shape how they are implemented. It says planning should involve stakeholders, especially key populations. It lists questions for targeting and implementing the national response, such as which subgroups are most at risk and what targets to set, and points to planning resources.

Explains that a practical monitoring and evaluation system is needed for the response among key populations, and lists WHO frameworks with national indicators on the enabling environment, coverage, quality and impact.

Explains how to set ambitious but realistic targets for intervention, outcome and impact indicators, involving stakeholders and using modelling. It covers baseline assessment and estimating the size of key populations. Methods such as census, surveys, capture-recapture and network scale-up are described, with triangulation advised.
A heading fragment for additional information on developing new recommendations.
Notes that the updated guidelines contain seven new recommendations or practice statements.

Describes how the seven new recommendations were developed, from PICO questions and outcome ranking to systematic reviews graded with GRADE and risk of bias tools. Four key population networks carried out qualitative research on values and preferences. Decisions were reached by consensus, with a two-thirds vote threshold agreed in advance, and drafts were reviewed in November 2021.

Presents the evidence and decision-making behind the new recommendations, beginning with counselling behavioural interventions to reduce HIV, STI and viral hepatitis risk among key populations. It explains why earlier recommendations needed updating and describes the systematic review and its outcomes. It continues through the other new recommendations with evidence summaries, values and preferences and implementation considerations. The end deals with research gaps, including economic evaluation of retesting in different settings.

The reference list (over 440 entries) for a WHO guideline on HIV, viral hepatitis and STI services for key populations, citing WHO strategies and guidelines alongside studies on HIV transmission, hepatitis C, drug use and STI testing methods such as pooled sampling.

Front matter of the 2022 WHO consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis and STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care for key populations, beginning with photo credits and the title page. It includes the copyright and cataloguing page with ISBNs and Creative Commons licence terms. A table of contents follows, listing chapters from the introduction and methods through critical enablers, service delivery and young key populations, and web annexes with values and preferences, systematic review findings and evidence-to-decision tables.
